messages.content: What is the difference between @Controller and @RestController?

@RestController is a convenience annotation that combines @Controller and @ResponseBody. With @Controller, handler return values are resolved as view names by default, so you add @ResponseBody to write the return value directly to the HTTP response body. @RestController applies @ResponseBody to every handler method, so return values are serialized (for example to JSON via Jackson) without a view.
What does spring.jpa.open-in-view do and why is it often disabled?

Open Session in View keeps the JPA EntityManager open for the whole web request, so lazy associations can still be loaded while rendering the response. Spring Boot enables it by default and logs a warning. It is often disabled because it holds a database connection for the entire request, hides N+1 queries in the web layer, and blurs transaction boundaries. With it off, load what you need in the service layer using JOIN FETCH, entity graphs or DTO projections.
What is the difference between findById and getReferenceById in Spring Data JPA?

findById hits the database immediately and returns an Optional that is empty if the row does not exist. getReferenceById returns a lazy proxy without querying; the database is only accessed when you touch a non-id field, and if the row is missing you get an EntityNotFoundException at that point. getReferenceById is useful for setting a foreign-key association without loading the referenced entity.
How does optimistic locking work in JPA?

Add a field annotated with @Version to the entity. On every update, JPA adds the version to the WHERE clause and increments it, for example UPDATE ... SET version = 6 WHERE id = ? AND version = 5. If another transaction already changed the row, zero rows are updated and an OptimisticLockException (ObjectOptimisticLockingFailureException in Spring) is thrown. It avoids holding database locks and suits low-contention data; the caller typically retries or reports a conflict.
What is the difference between @Bean and @Component?

@Component is placed on a class and the bean is discovered through component scanning, so it only works for classes you own. @Bean is placed on a method inside a @Configuration class and the method's return value becomes the bean, which lets you register third-party classes and control construction logic explicitly. Both produce singleton beans by default.
How do you run code once when a Spring Boot application starts?

Implement CommandLineRunner or ApplicationRunner as a bean; its run method is called after the application context has started. Alternatively, listen for ApplicationReadyEvent with @EventListener, which fires when the application is ready to serve requests. @PostConstruct runs earlier, right after a single bean is initialized, so it should not depend on the whole context being ready.
Why should you avoid using a JPA entity directly as a REST response?

Returning entities couples the API contract to the database schema, so a schema change can break clients. Serializing entities can trigger lazy loading (N+1 queries or LazyInitializationException) and infinite recursion on bidirectional relations. It can also leak internal or sensitive fields. Mapping to DTOs or records gives a stable, explicit contract and lets you fetch exactly the data needed.
What is the difference between Propagation.REQUIRED and Propagation.NESTED?

REQUIRED joins the existing transaction, so if the inner method fails and the exception propagates, the whole transaction is rolled back. NESTED runs inside the existing transaction but creates a savepoint; if the inner work fails, only changes since the savepoint are rolled back and the outer transaction can continue. NESTED needs savepoint support in the transaction manager. It works reliably with plain JDBC (DataSourceTransactionManager); with JPA the savepoint rolls back database changes but not the persistence context's in-memory state, so it is rarely a good fit there.
